claims.text: The multi-principal-element design of high-entropy alloys inherently promotes local chemical ordering.
The multi-principal-element design inherently produces a high density of grain boundaries.
Local chemical ordering and a high grain-boundary density enable rapid formation of a continuous Cr-rich protective oxide.
CrTaO4 or Cr2O3 can constitute the proposed protective Cr-rich oxide.
Chromium preferentially diffuses along grain boundaries to form the protective scale.
Sluggish bulk diffusion in HEAs limits further cation migration.
The resulting oxide scale is adherent and self-healing.
A continuous protective scale reduces both inward oxygen transport and outward transport of alloying elements.
The proposed test material is an equimolar CrMnFeCoNi or similar HEA processed to have an ultrafine-grained microstructure and local chemical ordering.
The controlled comparison uses a conventional alloy with a similar concentration of oxide-forming elements but without a multi-principal-element design.
The oxidation test is conducted in air at approximately 1000 °C for approximately 200 hours.
High grain-boundary density provides short-circuit diffusion paths, while local chemical ordering biases selective oxidation.
The balance between fast grain-boundary Cr transport and slow bulk transport promotes a coherent, continuous Cr-rich barrier.
Relative to the conventional-alloy baseline, the HEA will develop a more uniform, adherent, continuous Cr-rich scale and exhibit lower weight gain.
The conventional baseline will form a more heterogeneous, discontinuous mixed oxide and oxidize faster.
The mechanism applies near 1000 °C to alloys processed to have high grain-boundary densities and may change substantially with composition or grain refinement.
Existing evidence supports a qualitative role for grain-boundary density in forming protective Cr-rich oxide, but does not establish the role of local chemical ordering.
Failure of the HEA to produce a significantly more continuous Cr-rich scale with lower weight gain than the conventional control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: CrTaO4 is offered as an example of the protective oxide, but the explicitly named CrMnFeCoNi starting alloy contains no Ta and therefore cannot form CrTaO4 without an unstated composition change.

The hypothesis and mechanism attribute high grain-boundary density to inherent multi-element complexity, whereas the initial state and boundary fields attribute it to deliberate ultrafine-grain processing. The cited evidence supports processing-induced refinement rather than an inherent consequence of multi-principal-element chemistry.
